opening_summary: Nineteen terms about game design, from meaningful play and agency to risk, trade-offs, fairness, luck, balance and downtime. With the exact term you can tell a playtester, or an AI coding agent, what to change.
opening_description: 19 terms on choices, challenge and balance.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often say a hard game is an unfair game. It is not. Difficulty is how hard the opposition is. Fairness is whether the player can learn from losing. A game can be very hard and still fair. This film goes through nineteen terms on choices and challenge, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

beats.narration: This table is the map. Nineteen terms about game design, in four groups. The first group is choices that matter. Meaningful play, both descriptive and evaluative, meaningful choice, and agency. These terms ask whether the player's action means something.

The second group is kinds of interesting decision. Risk versus reward, trade-off, persistence, situational choice, personalisation and unit differentiation. These terms say what makes one decision more interesting than another.
The third group is the challenge. Frustration, difficulty, fairness, and luck and skill. These terms ask how hard a game is, and whether the player can learn from losing.
The fourth group is balance and waiting. Balance, rock-paper-scissors, downtime and probability. These terms ask whether every option, and every turn, is worth taking.

A red bola flies across and hits a block of ice, and the ice shatters. Meaningful play means the player acts and the game responds in a way that matters. Descriptive play is the first half of that, an action followed by a clear response the player sees at once. For example, in a platformer you build, the player stomps an enemy, it flattens with a squash sound, and the way ahead is clear.

Now a chain of five boxes runs from throw bola to finish game, with a red arc joining the ends. Evaluative play is the player stepping back to ask why an action matters to the whole game. Here the one throw is four steps from finishing. For example, a player realises that the key picked up in the first room is what opens the door before the goal flag, so the detour mattered.

Two lines branch through three forks. Agency, also called autonomy, means the player takes control of how the game is played. Three forks with two ways each make eight possible routes, two times two times two, and the red player and the black player finish the same level by different ones. For example, give your level a high path over the spikes and a low path under them, and let each player decide which way to go.

Bars of points. Risk versus reward means a harder or riskier action pays more, and the player weighs the factors before trying it. In this made-up example an invader is worth ten to thirty points, while the UFO, which is harder to hit, gives fifty to one hundred fifty, and three hundred on the twenty-third shot. For example, put a coin on a narrow ledge right above the spikes and make it worth more than the coins on the safe path.

Three situations, each scored as reward minus cost. A Meaningful choice changes what happens, and the player has to think about it. In this made-up example the same UFO scores plus twenty-five point five when the player is behind, minus seventeen when the invaders are near, and plus three on the last life. For example, a player on one heart has to think hard about jumping for a bonus coin over a pit, while a player on full health may simply go for it.

A score line over time. A Trade-off means giving up one thing to get another. In this made-up example the grey player scores a steady ten points a second. The red player gives up a ship at eight seconds, rescues it for dual fire, then scores twenty a second, and pulls ahead after eighteen seconds. For example, offer the player a heavy shield that blocks every hit but makes them jump lower.

Eight moments in a stage, and four power pellets. Persistence means the player has to carry the consequences of a choice for a set time. Here all four pellets go on the first four moments, the red boxes, so at the big group of ghosts none are left until the next stage. For example, if the player spends all of the level's bombs on the first few enemies, the boss at the end has to be fought without them.

A grid of enemies, sorted by how they move and how they attack. Unit differentiation, also called orthogonal unit differentiation, means each enemy type does something different, which forces the player to prioritise. The imp charges and its fireballs can be dodged, the cacodemon stays back, and the shotgun guy never misses. For example, give your platformer one enemy that rushes the player along a ledge and another that throws rocks from far away.

Bars now rank the threat you cannot dodge. Situational choice means the same choice is better or worse depending on the situation the player is in. In this made-up example the shotgun guy deals ten damage a second that cannot be dodged, the cacodemon three, and the imp two point five, so the shotgun guy goes first. For example, with a turret and a walking enemy in the room, break the turret first, but with walkers alone, jumping over them may be better.

Three rows of decisions, red for a risky pick and black for a safe one. Personalisation means players build their own play style from the decisions they make. All three face the same twenty decisions, and each chooses a different mix. For example, in a level with an optional enemy in every room, one player fights each one while another sneaks past them all, and both reach the goal.

Now each row is counted, in this simulated run. The aggressive player took the risky pick sixteen times out of twenty, eighty percent. The mixed player, eleven, fifty-five percent. The cautious player, three, fifteen percent. That spread of styles is personalisation. For example, the playtest notes for your platformer might show one tester always taking the spike path for the bonus coins, and another never taking it.

A chart of the chance of winning on each attempt, attempts one to twelve. Frustration is part of any challenge, but it has to be the kind the player can learn from. The red player learns, and wins in about two point eight attempts. The black player faces an inconsistent game, needs about ten, and learns nothing. For example, missing a jump because you misjudged the gap is frustration you learn from. Missing it because the platform's edge is invisible is not.

A grid of difficulty against fairness. Difficulty is how hard the opposition is. Fairness means clear expectations and consistent design, so the player can learn from failing. The two are separate. Hard and fair is satisfying to win, and hard and unfair feels cheap. For example, making the gaps in your level wider raises the difficulty. Hiding a spike under a landing spot, with no warning, makes the level unfair.

Bars for how often a skilled player beats a weaker one, in this simulated run. Luck and skill are the two things that decide a result. With luck, chance decides. With skill, the player's ability decides, and most games mix the two. In Candy Land, all luck, the stronger player wins fifty percent of the time. For example, a random item from a mystery box is luck, while timing a jump over a gap is skill.

A battle royale mixes the two, with random loot and skilled fights. Chance is weighted at sixty percent and skill at forty, and the skilled player wins sixty-two percent of matches. Luck still lets the weaker player win some of the time. For example, a platformer that hands out a random power-up at the start of each level, while every jump still takes skill, mixes luck and skill in the same way.

Counter-Strike is mostly skill. Chance is weighted at thirty percent and skill at seventy, and the skilled player wins eighty-six percent of matches. These weights are only an illustration. The point is that less luck lets the better player win more often. For example, if testers say your level feels random, put the power-ups in fixed places instead of random ones, so skill decides more of the result.

A triangle. Water beats fire, fire beats grass, grass beats water. Balance means every advantage has a disadvantage, so no role starts with an unfair edge. Rock-paper-scissors is one way to get it. Each option beats one and loses to another, so each wins zero point five against a random opponent. For example, in your game a knight beats an archer, the archer beats a mage, and the mage beats the knight, so no class is best.

After a change, fire and water now tie. Against a random opponent fire now wins zero point six seven, and water drops to zero point three three. Fire has an edge with no cost, so the balance is broken, and nobody picks water any more. For example, make the knight tie with the mage, and the mage loses the one fight it used to win, so players stop choosing it.

Two rows of turns for four players, with player one in red. Downtime is time a player waits with nothing to do. With turns of fifteen seconds, player one waits forty-five seconds between goes. With turns of forty-five seconds, the wait grows to one hundred thirty-five. For example, in a mode where two friends take turns at your level, keep each attempt short, or give the waiting player something to do.

Bars for the totals of two six-sided dice, grey for one roll and red for the better of two. Probability is the odds of each result, and extra rolls change them. A total of ten or more comes up sixteen point seven percent of the time on one roll, and thirty point six percent with the better of two. For example, if a chest in your level rarely gives a special item, letting the player open it twice makes that item far more likely.

Four look-alike pairs. Difficulty is how hard the opposition is, and the dark bar climbs to a hundred. Fairness is whether the player can learn from losing, and the red line rises as the player learns. A game can be very hard and still fair.
A Trade-off is giving up one thing to get another. One swap, and it is done. Persistence is living with a choice for a set time. The four circles, once spent, stay spent for the whole stage.

Luck is when chance decides the result. On the left the skilled player's wins, the filled squares, come only part of the time. Skill is when the player's ability decides it. On the right the skilled player nearly always wins.

Descriptive play is the game answering an action. A throw, and the box responds at once. Evaluative play is the player asking why the action matters. The chain of boxes runs all the way to the end of the game.

Each vague request becomes an exact instruction. Make the fights more interesting becomes, give each enemy a different behaviour. One charges and one stays back, one can be dodged and one never misses. Three enemies, three threat levels.
The shop is too easy to ignore becomes, make the choice persist. Robbing the shop sends a shopkeeper to the end of every level. The choice lasts, and the shopkeeper waits.

The game is too random becomes, cut luck to thirty percent, with random start loot only and skill deciding most fights. At sixty percent luck the skilled player wins sixty-two percent of matches. At thirty percent, eighty-six.
Waiting for turns is boring becomes, turns average fifteen seconds, one roll each, and give the others something to do. The wait between turns is forty-five seconds, not one hundred thirty-five.
The boss feels unfair becomes, same attack, same damage every time, so the player can learn it. The red dots jump around between five and forty damage. The dark dots stay at ten, every time.
This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you call the choices done. First, does the player see a response to each action, and understand why it matters?
Second, is there at least one real trade-off, or one lasting choice that stays with the player for a while?
Third, do different enemies or options call for different answers? That is unit differentiation, and it is one thing that makes a situational choice possible.
Fourth, is the challenge hard and fair, so that failing teaches something? The difficulty can be high, as long as the fairness holds.
Fifth, is the mix of luck and skill right for this game? More luck lets weaker players win, and more skill rewards practice.
Sixth, is every option worth taking, and are turns short enough to keep downtime low? Then say it exactly. Not make fights interesting, but one enemy never misses.

recap_lines: Descriptive play shows a response, and evaluative play asks why it matters.
Risk versus reward pays more for the harder, riskier action.
A trade-off is one swap, and persistence makes a choice stick for a set time.
Situational choice depends on the moment, personalisation on the player's style.
Difficulty is how hard it is, and fairness is whether you can learn from losing.
Rock-paper-scissors keeps options balanced, and short turns keep downtime low.

your_turn.command: Quiz me on game design terms with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use descriptive play, evaluative play, agency, risk versus reward, trade-off, persistence, situational choice, personalisation, difficulty and fairness. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.
checks: Check: each case is a game-making situation, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.

deck_problems: Slide 8 (Luck and skill) steps 2 and 3: the right-hand captions are one step out of sync with the bars. Step 2 adds the battle royale bar at 62% but its caption says 'Mostly skill: the stronger player wins 86% of matches.' Step 3 adds the Counter-Strike bar at 86% but its caption says 'A mix: 62%. A weaker player can still win with good loot...'. In renderLuck the second and third entries of the note array are swapped. The narration follows the bars.

Slide 4 step 1: the caption says the safe player 'scores slower after about 17 s' (a typed-in string), while the chart, computed from the same curves, says 'pays off after 18 s' (80 + 20(t - 13) = 10t gives t = 18). The sentence is also off in meaning: the safe player scores slower from the rescue at 13 s; at 18 s the trade player's total overtakes. The narration says eighteen seconds.

Slide 5 step 1: the caption ends 'Each differs from the others on both counts.' The grid says otherwise: imp and cacodemon are both dodgeable, and cacodemon and shotgun guy both stay back. Each enemy is in a different cell, but pairs share one count. The row label 'never misses' is also clipped to 'never miss' by the grid box.

Slide 11 step 3: the Luck panel caption says 'skilled player wins about half', but the drawn squares show the skilled player winning 3 of 12 (seeded draw), a quarter. The narration says 'only part of the time'.

Slide 11 step 2: the Trade-off and Persistence panels animate the same way (four shapes emptying one after another), so the picture does not show the difference the captions claim ('one swap, done' against 'spent for the whole stage').
Slide 12 step 2: the chart for the shopkeeper instruction reuses the power-pellet picture from slide 4, with the line 'first four moments: pellets gone', which is not about the shop.
Slide 12 step 5: the label 'consistent: damage 10 every time' is drawn across the red dots of the unpredictable row above it.

Slide 3 is badged Illustrative data and its note says 'All inputs illustrative', but the invader and UFO points (10/20/30, 50/100/150, 300 on the 23rd shot) are the real Space Invaders values cited from the source video. The narration follows the badge and says 'made-up example' once; the badge or the note could say which numbers come from the source.
Slide 4 step 2: two of the four 'moments' the pellets are spent on are a cherry and a 'blue ghost'; neither needs a power pellet, so the example reads oddly.

Term name varies: the term is 'Personalisation' (slides 1 and 6) but the TELL THESE APART boxes on slides 5 and 6 say 'Personal choice'. The map lists 'unit differentiation' while slide 5 also gives 'orthogonal unit differentiation'.
